renders._yaml:
- component: multiqc
  title: Adapter trimming and read collapsing
  description: |-
    AdapterRemoval's own MultiQC plot: for each sample, how many reads were kept, discarded or collapsed into a single merged read. It answers how much of the library was lost to trimming and how much of it merged.
    How to read: A high retained share means clean libraries. A large discarded share points to adapter dimers or very short inserts, so check the library preparation. A high collapsed share is expected for short inserts and is not a defect.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/adapterremoval
  section: adapterremoval

- component: multiqc
  title: ATAC library quality
  description: |-
    ataqv's own MultiQC plots: the fragment-length ladder, the peak-enrichment percentiles, the MAPQ spread and the per-chromosome read distribution, one line or bar per sample. They answer whether an ATAC library shows the expected nucleosomal structure and signal in peaks.
    How to read: A good library shows a nucleosome-free peak followed by mono- and di-nucleosome peaks, and a sharp rise of reads in peaks. A flat ladder or reads piled on mitochondrial or unplaced contigs point to over-transposition, low enrichment or contamination.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ataqv
  section: ataqv

- component: multiqc
  title: Variant-call statistics
  description: |-
    bcftools stats plots: substitution types, indel lengths and variant-quality counts per sample. They answer whether the call set has the profile of a healthy variant caller.
    How to read: Transitions should outnumber transversions. Indel lengths should fall off smoothly and frameshifting lengths should be rarer in coding regions. A sample whose profile departs from its peers deserves a look at its input quality.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/bcftools
  section: bcftools

- component: multiqc
  title: Demultiplexing statistics
  description: |-
    bcl2fastq's lane and sample summaries: how the reads of each lane were assigned to libraries, and which barcodes stayed undetermined. It answers whether the pool was loaded evenly and the indexes were read cleanly.
    How to read: Samples should receive similar read counts, and the undetermined share should be small. A large undetermined fraction or one dominant unknown barcode suggests a sample sheet mistake or index errors, so check the barcodes first.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/bcl2fastq/bcl2fastq.py
  section: bcl2fastq

- component: multiqc
  title: Bisulfite alignment QC
  description: |-
    Bismark's own MultiQC plots: alignment outcome, deduplication, strand specificity, M-bias and the methylation-extraction table per sample. They answer whether bisulfite reads aligned well and whether methylation calls are unbiased.
    How to read: A high unique-alignment rate and balanced strands are good. An M-bias curve that departs from flat at the read ends signals bias, which is usually fixed by clipping those positions before calling. High duplication reduces usable coverage.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/bismark
  section: bismark

- component: multiqc
  title: Alignment summary
  description: |-
    Bowtie 2's alignment summary: the share of read pairs aligned zero, one or several times, one bar per sample. It answers how well the reads map to the reference.
    How to read: A high concordant unique share is good. Many unaligned pairs point to contamination, the wrong reference or poor reads, and many multi-mapped pairs to repeats. Compare the samples and investigate the outliers.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/bowtie2
  section: bowtie2

- component: multiqc
  title: Abundance re-estimation
  description: |-
    Bracken's MultiQC plot: the top taxa after re-estimating abundance from the Kraken 2 report at one rank, as a stacked bar per sample. It answers which taxa dominate each library.
    How to read: The expected organisms should dominate and the unclassified share should be modest. Unexpected taxa across all samples can come from reagent contamination, so compare against negative controls where you have them.
    Sources: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/kraken and https://raw.githubusercontent.com/jenniferlu717/Bracken/master/README.md
  section: bracken

- component: multiqc
  title: CCS ZMW filtering
  description: |-
    PacBio ccs summary: how many ZMWs of each chunk gave a consensus read and why the others were filtered. It answers how much of the raw yield survived consensus calling.
    How to read: A high share of passing ZMWs is good. A large share filtered for low predicted accuracy or too few passes points to a short or damaged library, so revisit the preparation and loading.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ccs
  section: ccs

- component: multiqc
  title: Cell Ranger count summary
  description: |-
    Cell Ranger count's own MultiQC output: a per-sample summary table, the barcode-rank plot, and the median-genes-per-cell and sequencing-saturation curves. They answer whether each library captured enough real cells with enough depth.
    How to read: A barcode-rank plot with a clear cliff separates cells from background. Saturation that is still climbing means more sequencing would find more genes per cell. A low fraction of reads in cells or a missing cliff points to ambient RNA or a failed capture.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/cellranger
  section: cellranger

- component: multiqc
  title: Read classification (Centrifuge)
  description: |-
    Centrifuge's MultiQC plot: the top taxa of each library, classified against a compressed index, as a stacked bar per sample. It answers which organisms the reads come from.
    How to read: The expected organisms should dominate. A large unclassified share means the index lacks the organisms present. Unexpected taxa seen in every sample suggest a contaminant.
    Source: https://ccb.jhu.edu/software/centrifuge/
  section: centrifuge

- component: multiqc
  title: Bin quality (CheckM2)
  description: |-
    CheckM2's completeness and contamination estimates for each bin, shown as bars per bin. It answers which metagenome-assembled genomes are complete and clean enough to use.
    How to read: High completeness with low contamination marks a trustworthy bin. High contamination means the bin mixes organisms and should be refined, and low completeness means a fragment of a genome.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/checkm2
  section: checkm2

- component: multiqc
  title: Run QC verdicts
  description: |-
    CheckQC's pass or fail verdicts on reads per sample, undetermined share and overrepresented unknown indexes. It answers whether the sequencing run met its own quality handbook.
    How to read: Passing checks mean the run is fit to analyse. A failed check names the lane or sample that missed its limit, so look at the run quality before using that data.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/checkqc
  section: checkqc

- component: multiqc
  title: Adapter trimming
  description: |-
    Cutadapt's MultiQC plots: how many reads were filtered and the lengths of the trimmed sequences, per sample. They answer how much adapter was found and how much was removed.
    How to read: A moderate trimmed share is routine. A trimmed-length peak far from the adapter's true length hints at the wrong adapter, and a very high trimmed share suggests short inserts or adapter dimers.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/cutadapt
  section: cutadapt

- component: multiqc
  title: Ancient-DNA damage (MultiQC)
  description: |-
    DamageProfiler's own MultiQC plots: 5' and 3' misincorporation curves and read-length distributions, one line per sample. They answer whether the reads carry the cytosine deamination signature of ancient DNA.
    How to read: Authentic ancient DNA shows C to T substitutions rising toward the 5' end and G to A toward the 3' end of double-stranded libraries, with short reads. A flat profile suggests modern contamination or a library repaired by enzymatic treatment.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/damageprofiler/damageprofiler.py
  section: damageprofiler

- component: multiqc
  title: Signal enrichment
  description: |-
    deepTools plotFingerprint curve: the cumulative share of signal against the share of the genome covered, one curve per sample. It answers whether a ChIP sample is enriched over its input.
    How to read: An input or a failed ChIP follows the diagonal. An enriched sample bows toward the lower right because a few regions hold most of the signal, and the further it bows the stronger the enrichment.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/deeptools
  section: deeptools

- component: multiqc
  title: Duplication vs expression
  description: |-
    dupRadar's curve of the duplication rate against gene expression, one line or scatter per sample. It answers whether duplicates are natural, from highly expressed genes, or an artefact of library preparation.
    How to read: Duplication should rise only for the most expressed genes. A high rate across the whole range signals low input or over-amplification, and these reads should not be removed blindly in RNA-seq.
    Source: https://bioconductor.org/packages/release/bioc/html/dupRadar.html
  section: dupradar

- component: multiqc
  title: Raw-read QC (Falco)
  description: |-
    Falco's own MultiQC plots, a FastQC reimplementation: per-base quality, GC content, duplication and adapter content per sample. They answer whether the demultiplexed reads are fit to analyse.
    How to read: Quality should stay high along the read and adapter content should be near zero. A GC profile with an extra peak points to contamination, and falling quality at the 3' end to a run problem, so trim or resequence.
    Lines and annotations: The per-base quality plot is banded green, orange and red at the Phred 28 and 20 limits used by MultiQC's FastQC plots, and the adapter plot is banded the same way by percentage of reads.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/fastqc/fastqc.py
  section: falco

- component: multiqc
  title: Read pre-processing
  description: |-
    fastp's MultiQC plots: filtering outcome, insert-size distribution and GC and N content per sample. They answer how much of the library was removed and how the retained reads look.
    How to read: Most reads should pass the filters. A broad or double-peaked insert size can mean adapter read-through, and a high N content points to a sequencing problem.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/fastp
  section: fastp

- component: multiqc
  title: Raw-read QC
  description: |-
    FastQC's own plots aggregated by MultiQC: per-base quality, GC content, duplication and adapter content, one line per sample. They answer whether the raw reads are fit for downstream analysis.
    How to read: Quality should stay in the green band along the read and adapter content should be near zero. A shifted or multi-peaked GC curve suggests contamination, so check the sample before trusting its results.
    Lines and annotations: The per-base and per-sequence quality plots are banded green above a Phred score of 28, orange from 20 to 28 and red below 20. The adapter content plot is banded orange from 5 to 20 percent and red above 20 percent. The bands are set in the MultiQC FastQC module.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/fastqc/fastqc.py
  section: fastqc

- component: multiqc
  title: Read assignment
  description: |-
    featureCounts' MultiQC plot: how many reads were assigned to a feature and why the rest were not (no feature, ambiguity, multimapping), one bar per sample. It answers how much of the library can be counted.
    How to read: A high assigned share is good. A large no-feature share points to the wrong annotation or genomic DNA, and a large multimapping share to repeats.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/featurecounts
  section: featurecounts

- component: multiqc
  title: FRiP score
  description: |-
    The fraction of reads in peaks (FRiP): the share of mapped reads that fall inside called peaks, one bar per sample. It answers how well a sample's signal concentrates in peaks.
    How to read: Higher is better because more of the library is real signal. A low value means weak enrichment or too few peaks, so check the immunoprecipitation and the peak calling before interpreting the sample.
  section: frip

- component: multiqc
  title: Base quality recalibration
  description: |-
    GATK4's base quality score recalibration plots: observed against reported base quality after recalibration, per sample. They answer whether the sequencer's reported qualities match reality.
    How to read: Points should lie close to the diagonal after recalibration. Large departures mean the reported qualities were miscalibrated, which can bias variant calls.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/gatk
  section: gatk

- component: multiqc
  title: General statistics
  description: |-
    The table every MultiQC report has: one row per sample and one column per headline metric that each module contributed. It answers where a sample stands across all tools at once.
    How to read: Sort a column to find the outliers, then open the matching module section for detail. A sample that stands out on several columns is the one to inspect or exclude.
  section: general

- component: multiqc
  title: MAG taxonomy (GTDB-Tk)
  description: |-
    GTDB-Tk's taxonomic placement of each metagenome-assembled genome against the Genome Taxonomy Database, with the identity to the closest reference. It answers which organism each bin represents.
    How to read: A bin placed to species with a high identity to its reference is well characterised. A placement only to a high rank means the genome is novel or the bin is incomplete or mixed.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/gtdbtk
  section: gtdbtk

- component: multiqc
  title: Germline benchmark (hap.py)
  description: |-
    hap.py's accuracy summary per callset: precision, recall and F1 for SNPs and indels against a truth set. It answers how accurate a germline variant caller is.
    How to read: Values close to one are better. Low recall means missed true variants and low precision means false calls, and indels are usually harder than SNPs.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/happy/happy.py
  section: happy

- component: multiqc
  title: HiC-Pro mapping and filtering
  description: |-
    HiC-Pro's MultiQC plots: read mapping, pairing, valid-pair filtering and contact statistics per sample. They answer how many read pairs end up as usable chromatin contacts.
    How to read: A high share of valid interaction pairs is good. Many dangling ends or self-circles point to inefficient ligation or digestion, which lowers usable depth.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/hicpro
  section: hicpro

- component: multiqc
  title: Primer trimming
  description: |-
    iVar's amplicon primer-trimming and variant metrics per sample. They answer how many reads had primers removed and how the called variants look.
    How to read: Most mapped reads should be trimmed in an amplicon protocol. A low trimmed share means the primer scheme does not match the reads, which can leave primer sequence in variant calls.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ivar
  section: ivar

- component: multiqc
  title: Protein-level classification
  description: |-
    Kaiju's MultiQC plot: the top taxa from protein-level classification of reads, as a stacked bar per sample. It answers which organisms the reads come from, including distant ones.
    How to read: The expected organisms should dominate and the unclassified share should be modest. Protein-level matching reaches deeper than nucleotide matching, so a high unclassified share still points to a novel community or a poor database.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/kaiju
  section: kaiju

- component: multiqc
  title: Read classification
  description: |-
    Kraken 2's MultiQC plot: the top taxa of each library as a stacked bar per sample. It answers which species or clades the reads come from.
    How to read: The expected organisms should dominate. A large unclassified share means the database misses what is present, and unexpected taxa across all samples suggest contamination.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/kraken
  section: kraken

- component: multiqc
  title: Lima primer demultiplexing
  description: |-
    PacBio lima's summary: how many CCS reads of each chunk carried a valid primer pair and why the others were rejected. It answers how much of the yield could be assigned to a barcode.
    How to read: A high share of passing reads is good. Many rejected for missing or mismatched primers point to a wrong primer file, or to a library with chimeric or incomplete molecules.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/lima
  section: lima

- component: multiqc
  title: Metagenomic alignment
  description: |-
    MALT's MultiQC plot: how many queries aligned at all and how many of those received a taxonomic assignment, per sample. It answers how much of the library the reference database explains.
    How to read: A high assigned share means the database fits the sample. A low share means a divergent or poorly represented community, and low specificity of the hits to the taxon.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/malt
  section: malt

- component: multiqc
  title: Marker-gene profile
  description: |-
    MetaPhlAn's MultiQC plot: the top taxa from clade-specific marker genes, as a stacked bar per sample. It answers the composition of the microbial community.
    How to read: Profiles of similar samples should look alike. A taxon absent from most samples but dominant in one is worth checking for contamination or a real difference.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/metaphlan
  section: metaphlan

- component: multiqc
  title: isomiR counts
  description: |-
    mirtop's counts of isomiRs per variant type: reference, 3p and 5p end changes, non-templated additions and nucleotide changes, per sample. They answer how much miRNA sequence variation the library holds.
    How to read: Reference sequences and 3p variants usually dominate. A sample with an unusual variant mix may reflect a trimming or mapping issue rather than biology.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/mirtop/mirtop.py
  section: mirtop

- component: multiqc
  title: Small RNA library QC
  description: |-
    miRTrace's own MultiQC plots: read QC outcome, RNA type composition, read length, clade contamination check and miRNA complexity per sample. They answer whether a small RNA library is clean and complex enough.
    How to read: A clean library has most reads passing, a high miRNA share and a length peak near 22 nucleotides, the typical miRNA length. Reads from another clade suggest contamination, and a flat complexity curve says deeper sequencing finds few new miRNAs.
    Lines and annotations: The read length plot is banded at 18, 26 and 40 nucleotides, the length classes miRTrace uses, with the miRNA range from 18 to 26. The bands are drawn by the MultiQC miRTrace module.
    Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/mirtrace/mirtrace.py and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30514392/
  section: mirtrace

- component: advanced_viz
  id: complexity_curve
  title: miRNA complexity curve
  description: |-
    Each line is one library: the number of distinct miRNAs miRTrace detects in a subsample of the given size. It answers whether the library was sequenced deep enough to see its miRNAs.
    How to read: a curve that has flattened means deeper sequencing would add few new miRNAs. A curve still climbing at the library's full depth means the library is under-sequenced. Compare libraries of the same type: a curve that stays far below its peers points to a low-complexity library.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/mirtrace/mirtrace.py
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Reads sampled
    y_title: Distinct miRNAs detected
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: reads
    y: distinct_mirnas

- component: table
  title: Complexity values
  description: |-
    One row is one library at one sampled depth: the reads sampled and the distinct miRNAs found. It gives the exact values behind the curve and answers how many miRNAs each library reveals.
    How to read: sort by distinct miRNAs at the deepest depth to rank libraries by complexity, and look for those that plateau earliest, which are the least diverse. It complements the complexity curve tile.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: rna_composition
  title: Small RNA library composition
  description: |-
    Each bar is one library, split into the categories of the chosen breakdown: reads by RNA type, reads by miRTrace QC outcome, or detected miRNAs by organism clade. It answers whether the library holds the small RNAs it should and whether another organism contributes.
    How to read: a good small RNA library is dominated by miRNA among the RNA types and by reads passing QC. Detected miRNAs should come from the sample's own clade, and a notable share from another clade suggests contamination. Use the rank selector to switch between the three breakdowns.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/mirtrace/mirtrace.py
  kind: stacked_bar
  config:
    value_title: Share of library
  roles:
    sample_id: sample
    taxon: taxon
    rank: rank
    abundance: abundance

- component: interactive
  title: Breakdown
  description: 'Choose which of the three miRTrace breakdowns the other tiles show: RNA type, read QC outcome
    or clade. Selecting one keeps the stacked bars comparable, because each breakdown has its own categories.'
  interactive_type: MultiSelect
  column_name: rank

- component: table
  title: Composition values
  description: |-
    One row is one library, breakdown and category, with its count and its share of the breakdown. It gives the exact values behind the stacked bars and answers what each library is made of.
    How to read: sort by share to find the dominant categories, then filter to one breakdown to compare libraries. Look for a category whose share differs sharply between libraries. It complements the composition bars tile.

- component: advanced_viz
  id: length_profile
  title: Read length distribution
  description: |-
    Each line is one library: the share of its reads at each length after adapter removal. It answers whether the library is made of miRNA-sized fragments.
    How to read: a clean miRNA library peaks near 22 nt, the typical miRNA length named in the miRTrace paper. A pile-up below 18 nt points to adapter dimers or over-trimming, and a broad smear toward longer reads to degraded RNA. Libraries should overlay closely.
    Lines and annotations: the shaded band spans 18 to 26 nt, the length class miRTrace and MultiQC treat as miRNA in their length plot.
    Sources: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/mirtrace/mirtrace.py and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/30514392/
  kind: profile
  config:
    x_title: Read length (nt)
    y_title: Percent of library reads
    shaded_bands:
    - - 18
      - 26
      - miRNA range
  roles:
    series: sample
    x: length
    y: percent

- component: figure
  title: Read length per library
  description: |-
    Each line is one library: the share of its reads at each length, drawn as a plain line figure. It answers the same question as the profile above, with the figure's own zoom and legend controls.
    How to read: look for a peak near 22 nt and compare the libraries. A library whose peak sits elsewhere or is flat deserves a closer look.
  visu_type: line
  dict_kwargs:
    x: length
    y: percent
    color: sample
    labels:
      length: Read length (nt)
      percent: Percent of library reads
      sample: Library

- component: table
  title: Length values
  description: |-
    One row is one library at one read length, with its read count, its share of the library and the length class miRTrace assigns. It gives the exact values behind the curves and answers where each library's reads concentrate.
    How to read: sort by share to find each library's dominant length, and look for libraries whose peak sits at a different length from the rest. It complements the read length distribution tile.

- component: multiqc
  title: Coverage distribution
  description: |-
    mosdepth's MultiQC plots: the coverage distribution and coverage per contig, one line per sample. They answer how deeply and evenly the genome is covered.
    How to read: A narrow distribution around the target depth is good. A long tail at low coverage means gaps, and a second peak can mean copy-number changes or contamination.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/mosdepth
  section: mosdepth

- component: multiqc
  title: Long-read filtering
  description: |-
    nanoq's MultiQC plots: the read length and read quality distributions after filtering, per sample. They answer what the retained long-read library looks like.
    How to read: A length distribution with a long tail is typical for long reads. A quality distribution centred low means the library will need stricter filtering or better basecalling.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/nanoq
  section: nanoq

- component: multiqc
  title: Long-read QC
  description: |-
    NanoStat's summary of read length, read quality and yield, per sample, as MultiQC shows it. It answers whether the run produced enough usable long reads.
    How to read: A high N50 and a good mean quality are good. Low yield or short reads point to degraded DNA or a poor library preparation.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/nanostat
  section: nanostat

- component: multiqc
  title: Coverage redundancy
  description: |-
    Nonpareil's curves of metagenome coverage against sequencing effort, one line per sample. They answer how much of the community the sequencing has captured and how much more would be needed.
    How to read: A curve that flattens near full coverage means the sample is well sequenced. A curve still rising steeply means more sequencing would reveal new sequence.
    Lines and annotations: The ideal coverage and ideal sequencing effort are computed by Nonpareil from the model fit, as the MultiQC module describes.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/nonpareil
  section: nonpareil

- component: multiqc
  title: NSC coefficient
  description: |-
    The normalised strand cross-correlation (NSC) of each sample: the ratio of the fragment-length correlation peak to the background. It answers whether a ChIP or ATAC library carries any fragment-length enrichment.
    How to read: A value near one means no enrichment at all, and higher values mean stronger enrichment. Read it together with the RSC coefficient to tell real signal from a phantom peak.
  section: nsc

- component: multiqc
  title: Percolator feature weights
  description: |-
    The median weight Percolator gave each rescoring feature, per sample. It answers which features the rescoring relies on.
    How to read: A feature carrying most of the weight is the one the rescoring depends on. A shift of weight between samples is where a search or prediction model problem shows first.
  section: percolator

- component: multiqc
  title: Library and transcript metrics
  description: |-
    Picard's MultiQC plots: duplication, insert-size distribution, where the bases land across transcript regions and the gene-body coverage, per sample. They answer how well the library covers the transcriptome.
    How to read: A narrow insert-size peak, a high coding share and even gene-body coverage are good. Coverage piling up at one end of genes indicates RNA degradation or poly-A bias.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/picard
  section: picard

- component: multiqc
  title: Long-read adapter trimming
  description: |-
    Porechop_ABI's summary of reads and bases kept after adapter trimming, per sample. It answers how much of the long-read library carried adapters.
    How to read: Most reads should be kept. A very large trimmed share or many reads split in the middle suggest chimeric reads or a wrong adapter set.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/porechop
  section: porechop

- component: multiqc
  title: Library complexity
  description: |-
    Preseq's complexity curve: how many distinct molecules a library is predicted to yield for a given number of sequenced reads, one line per sample. It answers how many additional unique molecules each extra million reads buys.
    How to read: A steep curve means the library is far from saturation and deeper sequencing pays off. A curve that flattens early means a low-complexity library, where more reads mostly repeat what was seen.
    Lines and annotations: The dashed line shows a perfectly complex library in which each read is unique. It is drawn by the MultiQC Preseq module.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/preseq
  section: preseq

- component: multiqc
  title: Bin annotation (Prokka)
  description: |-
    Prokka's per-bin annotation summary: coding sequences, coding density and genome size. It answers whether each bin looks like a complete, well-annotated genome.
    How to read: Bacterial genomes are typically densely coding. A low gene count or unusual size points to a fragmentary or contaminated bin.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/prokka
  section: prokka

- component: multiqc
  title: Transcript coverage
  description: |-
    Qualimap's MultiQC plots: the genomic origin of the reads (exonic, intronic, intergenic) and the 5' to 3' gene-body coverage profile, per sample. They answer how the reads distribute across the transcriptome.
    How to read: Most reads should be exonic and the gene-body profile should be even. A strong 3' bias suggests RNA degradation, and many intergenic reads suggest genomic DNA.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/qualimap/QM_RNASeq.py
  section: qualimap

- component: multiqc
  title: Assembly quality
  description: |-
    QUAST's assembly metrics per assembly: contig counts and lengths. They answer how contiguous and complete an assembly is.
    How to read: Fewer, longer contigs and a high N50 are better. Many short contigs mean a fragmented assembly, and a total length far from the expected genome size points to contamination or missing sequence.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/quast
  section: quast

- component: multiqc
  title: Ribo-seq footprint quality
  description: |-
    Ribo-TISH's quality plots: reading-frame proportions and the read-length distribution of the footprints. They answer whether a Ribo-seq library shows ribosome periodicity.
    How to read: Genuine footprints concentrate in one reading frame and in a narrow length range. Even frame proportions mean little ribosome signal.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ribotish
  section: ribotish

- component: multiqc
  title: Ribo-seq periodicity
  description: |-
    riboWaltz's plots: the P-site distribution across transcript regions, the reading-frame distribution and the metagene profiles at the start and stop codons. They answer whether the footprints show three-nucleotide periodicity.
    How to read: Footprints should lie mostly in the coding region, favour one frame and peak at the start codon. Missing periodicity means the library or the P-site offsets are unreliable.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/ribowaltz
  section: ribowaltz

- component: multiqc
  title: RSC coefficient
  description: |-
    The relative strand cross-correlation (RSC) of each sample: the fragment-length correlation peak measured against the read-length artefact peak. It answers whether the signal is real enrichment or a phantom peak.
    How to read: Higher values mean the fragment-length peak clearly beats the read-length peak. A low value means the library is dominated by the artefact, so interpret the peaks with caution.
  section: rsc

- component: multiqc
  title: RNA-seq read QC
  description: |-
    RSeQC's MultiQC plots: read distribution over the transcriptome, inner distance, junction annotation and saturation, and strand inference, per sample. They answer how the reads map onto the gene models and whether the library is stranded.
    How to read: A high coding share, a clear strandedness call and junction saturation that levels off are good. A mixed strand call suggests an unstranded library or the wrong strandedness setting.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/rseqc
  section: rseqc

- component: multiqc
  title: Transcript quantification
  description: |-
    Salmon's MultiQC plots: the fragment-length distribution and the mapping rate, per sample. They answer how well the reads support the quantification.
    How to read: A smooth fragment-length distribution and a high mapping rate are good. A low mapping rate means contamination or an incomplete transcriptome.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/salmon
  section: salmon

- component: multiqc
  title: Alignment flagstats
  description: |-
    samtools flagstat's counts per sample: mapped and properly paired reads. They answer how well the reads align.
    How to read: A high mapped share and a high proper-pair share are good. Low values point to contamination, the wrong reference or poor library quality.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/samtools
  section: samtools

- component: multiqc
  title: Variant effects
  description: |-
    SnpEff's annotation summary: impact, class and region of the variants, per sample. They answer what kinds of changes the variants make.
    How to read: Most variants usually fall in non-coding or low-impact classes. Many high-impact calls in one sample are worth checking against its input quality.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/snpeff
  section: snpeff

- component: multiqc
  title: Somatic benchmark (som.py)
  description: |-
    som.py's accuracy tables per caller: recall, precision and the true positive, false negative and false positive counts for the combined, indel and SNV records. It answers how accurate a somatic caller is against a truth set.
    How to read: Values close to one are better. Low recall means missed variants and low precision means false calls, and indels are usually harder than SNVs.
    Source: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/MultiQC/MultiQC/main/multiqc/modules/sompy/sompy.py
  section: sompy

- component: multiqc
  title: rRNA removal
  description: |-
    SortMeRNA's MultiQC plot: the share of each library's reads matched to the rRNA databases and removed, per database. It answers how much ribosomal RNA the library held.
    How to read: A small rRNA share means the depletion worked. A high share leaves few informative reads, so check the depletion step.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/sortmerna
  section: sortmerna

- component: multiqc
  title: Splice-aware alignment summary
  description: |-
    STAR's MultiQC plots: the uniquely mapped, multi-mapped and unmapped fractions, plus per-gene count assignment, per sample. They answer how well the reads align to the genome.
    How to read: A high unique-mapping share is good. Many unmapped reads that are too short suggest degraded RNA, and many multi-mapped ones indicate repeats.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/star
  section: star

- component: multiqc
  title: Strand cross-correlation
  description: |-
    The cross-correlation between plus and minus strand read densities across strand shifts, one curve per sample. It answers how sharply the library is enriched at the fragment length.
    How to read: A clear peak at the fragment length means real enrichment. A peak at the read length alone is a phantom peak, so compare with the NSC and RSC coefficients.
  section: strand

- component: multiqc
  title: Pipeline summary
  description: |-
    Per-sample pipeline summary metrics, assembly and variant calling, as the viralrecon summary tables report them. They answer which samples produced a usable assembly and calls.
    How to read: Samples with good coverage and few ambiguous bases are usable. A sample that stands out on mapped reads or coverage should be checked before its variants are trusted.
  section: summary

- component: card
  title: Genome covered at 10x
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of the genome covered by at least 10 reads, and the box shows the spread. It answers whether the samples were sequenced deeply enough for confident variant calls.
    How to read: values near 100 percent mean the whole genome is callable. A sample far below the box has gaps, so its missing positions cannot be called and it deserves a look before its variants are trusted.
    Note: no pass mark is drawn, because the pipeline defines no cut-off for this metric.
  column: pct_genome_covered_10x
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Variants per sample
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median count of variants called per sample (SNPs and indels together), and the box shows the spread. It answers how divergent the samples are from the reference.
    How to read: samples of one lineage should carry similar counts. A sample far above its peers may be a mixed infection or a different lineage, and one far below may have poor coverage.
  column: num_variants_total
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: table
  title: Variant-calling summary
  description: |-
    One row is one sample: reads mapped, coverage, SNP, indel and total variant counts, and lineage. It gives the exact values behind the cards and answers which samples stand out.
    How to read: sort by genome coverage ascending to find the weakest samples, then by variant count to find unusual ones. Compare with the lineage composition tile to see whether an outlier belongs to a minority lineage.

- component: card
  title: Variants by lineage
  description: |-
    The hero number is the total count of variants called across all samples, and the bars rank the lineages that account for most of them. It answers which lineages carry the variant load.
    How to read: a lineage leading the ranking either has many samples or many variants per sample, so read it with the lineage composition tile.
  column: num_variants_total
  aggregation: sum
  aggregations:
  - max
  secondary_layout: top_n
  breakdown_col: lineage
  top_n_count: 3
  caption: variants, by lineage

- component: card
  title: Reads mapped
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of reads that mapped to the reference, and the box shows the spread. It answers how much of each library is usable for calling.
    How to read: a high value means a clean library on the right reference. A sample far below the box points to host or other contamination, or to a reference that does not match.
  column: pct_reads_mapped
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread
  headline: true

- component: card
  title: Weakest genome breadth at 10x
  description: |-
    The hero number is the lowest percent of the genome covered at 10x among the samples, and the histogram counts samples by that breadth. It answers whether any sample is thinly covered.
    How to read: a tight pile near 100 percent means every sample is deeply covered. A tail to the left holds the samples to rerun or exclude.
    Note: no pass mark is drawn, because the pipeline defines no cut-off for this metric.
  column: pct_genome_covered_10x
  aggregation: min
  aggregations:
  - median
  - max
  secondary_layout: histogram
  caption: samples, by breadth at 10x

- component: card
  title: Lineage composition
  description: |-
    The hero number is the count of samples, and the ring splits them by assigned lineage. It answers which lineages the batch contains and how evenly.
    How to read: one dominant lineage is typical of an outbreak. Many small slices mean a diverse batch, and a sample with no lineage assigned usually had too little coverage to classify.
  column: lineage
  aggregation: count
  aggregations:
  - nunique
  secondary_layout: donut
  breakdown_col: lineage
  caption: samples, by lineage

- component: card
  title: Genome covered at 1x
  description: |-
    The hero number is the median across samples of the percent of the genome covered by at least one read, and the box shows the spread. It answers whether the samples reach the whole genome at all, however thinly.
    How to read: a gap between this tile and the 10x tile means regions covered too thinly for calling. A sample low on both has large missing stretches.
  column: pct_genome_covered_1x
  aggregation: median
  aggregations:
  - box_plot_stats
  secondary_layout: box_plot
  caption: median, with its spread

- component: multiqc
  title: Structural-variant benchmark (Truvari)
  description: |-
    Truvari's accuracy summary per callset: precision against recall and the true-positive, false-positive and false-negative classes. It answers how accurate a structural-variant caller is against a truth set.
    How to read: Values close to one are better. A low recall means missed events and a low precision means false calls, and the breakdown by size shows where it fails.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/truvari
  section: truvari

- component: multiqc
  title: Ts/Tv by quality and count
  description: |-
    VCFtools' transition to transversion ratio as a function of variant quality and non-reference allele count. It answers whether the call quality tracks real variants.
    How to read: The ratio should be fairly stable across the range. A ratio that drops at low quality shows where false calls enter, which helps you choose a quality filter.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/vcftools
  section: vcftools

- component: multiqc
  title: Variant annotation
  description: |-
    Ensembl VEP's summary plots: consequence classes, SIFT and PolyPhen calls and chromosome distribution, per sample. They answer what the variants do to genes and proteins.
    How to read: Most variants are expected to be non-coding or synonymous. A skewed chromosome distribution or an excess of damaging calls deserves a check of the input.
    Source: https://docs.seqera.io/multiqc/modules/vep
  section: vep
